findings.title: hx_env_str returns NULL or "" for the same empty variable, depending on a stale GetLastError value
findings.evidence: For an empty value GetEnvironmentVariableW returns 0 and leaves the thread's last-error unchanged. The code then reads `got == 0 && GetLastError() == ERROR_ENVVAR_NOT_FOUND`, so an earlier lookup of an unset variable decides the result. Repro v_env.c: SetEnvironmentVariableW(L"HXV_EMPTY", L""), then hx_env_str("HXV_EMPTY"), then hx_env_str("HXV_DEFINITELY_UNSET"), then hx_env_str("HXV_EMPTY") again. Output: `empty var, fresh: "" | after an unset lookup: NULL`. POSIX getenv always returns "". The header says NULL only if the variable is unset.
findings.fix_hint: Call SetLastError(ERROR_SUCCESS) before each GetEnvironmentVariableW call, or treat need==1 / got==0 as an empty string.

findings.title: hx_f16_to_f32 keeps signalling NaNs signalling; F16C (used by the SIMD kernels) quiets them
findings.evidence: v_half_avx512.c compares all 65536 f16 patterns against _mm256_cvtph_ps (VCVTPH2PS). There are 1022 mismatches, all signalling NaNs: 0x7c01 gives 0x7f802000, hardware gives 0x7fc02000. quant_avx2.c and quant_avx512.c decode f16 with F16C, and quant.c had to write its own q_f16 ('identical to F16C vcvtph2ps (signalling NaNs come back quiet)') instead of using this function. Any scalar path that uses hx_f16_to_f32 next to F16C SIMD would differ bit-for-bit on these inputs (an INV-DET-3 hazard, NaN-only). f32->f16 and f32->bf16 are fine: 0 mismatches against VCVTPS2PH over all 2^32 inputs, and 0 against VCVTNEPS2BF16 for non-denormal inputs.
findings.fix_hint: In the exp==0x1f, mant!=0 branch also set the quiet bit (bits = sign | 0x7fc00000 | mant<<13) so the result matches F16C; update the round-trip expectation in test_platform.

findings.title: hx_cond_timedwait reports a timeout before the requested interval has passed
findings.evidence: v_platform_adv.c, minimum elapsed time with a return value of 1: 1000 us gave 976.5 us (5/40 returned early); 2000 us gave 1924.6 us (8/40); 5000 us gave 4970.2 us (8/40). The engineer's own test run printed 'timedwait(20 ms) -> 1 after 19.84 ms'. The contract_issues entry says the wait 'rounds up to whole milliseconds', which implies it never returns early; that is not what happens. The test's lower bound (>= 5 ms for a 20 ms wait) is too loose to catch this.
findings.fix_hint: Compute a deadline with hx_now_ns and re-wait for the remaining time until it passes before returning 1, or document that the wait can end up to one tick early.

findings.title: Windows CPU counts ignore process affinity; POSIX respects it
findings.evidence: `cmd /c start /affinity 3 /wait v_cpus.exe` printed hx_num_cpus=32 and hx_num_physical_cores=16, the same as without the restriction. platform_posix.c uses sched_getaffinity and clamps the core count to it. A pool sized from these numbers in an affinity-limited process or job object gets more threads than CPUs, and spinning pools degrade badly in that case (measured at 32 threads on 32 CPUs: mean 146-412 us, p99 about 1.1 ms).
findings.fix_hint: Use GetProcessAffinityMask (or GetProcessGroupAffinity / CPU sets) and count only cores whose GROUP_AFFINITY.Mask intersects the process mask.

findings.title: test_platform fails spuriously when HEARTH_LOG has surrounding whitespace
findings.evidence: Running `HEARTH_LOG=' 2 ' v_test_platform.exe` prints 'FAIL ... test_platform.c:835: initial log level 2 (HEARTH_LOG= 2 ), want 1'. The library accepts surrounding whitespace (hx__parse_ll, the same rule as hx_env_int), but the test's own expectation parser requires *end == 0. The other values 0, 2, 3, 9, -1, junk and '' all pass.
findings.fix_hint: Skip trailing whitespace in the test's parser, or only use the HEARTH_LOG values the test controls.

findings.title: Windows env cache grows without bound and lookups get quadratically slower
findings.evidence: Every distinct (name, value) pair is kept for the life of the process in a linked list that is searched linearly. v_envchurn.c: 10k distinct values took 0.29 s, 20k took 0.88 s, and the batch from 40k to 80k took 14.15 s. This is only a problem if something polls a variable whose value keeps changing.
findings.fix_hint: Keep only the latest value per name and retire older strings to a short free-later list, or use a small hash table; document the pointer lifetime in the header.

findings.title: hx_env_double depends on the host's numeric locale
findings.evidence: v_locale.c: HXV_D=0.25 parses to 0.25 in the C locale. After setlocale(LC_NUMERIC, "de-DE"), hx_env_double returns the default -1 and logs 'ignoring HXV_D="0.25": not a number'. hearth.dll can be loaded into host processes whose locale it does not control.
findings.fix_hint: Parse with a locale-independent routine (_strtod_l with a C locale on Windows, strtod_l/uselocale on POSIX), or with a small custom decimal parser.

findings.title: macOS x86-64 will report no AVX-512, because Darwin enables AVX-512 state lazily (found by reading the code)
findings.evidence: zmm_ok requires XCR0 & 0xe0. On Darwin the kernel sets the opmask/ZMM bits in XCR0 only after a thread's first AVX-512 instruction, which is why LLVM's Host.cpp trusts CPUID on __APPLE__. On AVX-512 Intel Macs every avx512* flag would read 0 and the AVX2 kernels would be used. Output stays identical (INV-DET-3); only speed is lost. Not compiled here: no macOS toolchain.
findings.fix_hint: Under __APPLE__ x86-64, take AVX-512 from CPUID when the OS reports XSAVE support, or query sysctl hw.optional.avx512f.

findings.title: Test gaps: loose timing bounds and no INT64_MAX offset boundary case
findings.evidence: (a) The hx_sleep_us 'far too early' bound is us/2 - 100 us, and the timedwait bound is >= 5 ms for a 20 ms request, so the early timeout above passes unnoticed. findings.title: Signed left-shift overflow (undefined behaviour) in the AVX2 BF16 tail path; UBSan reports it on every test_quant run
findings.evidence: w_one(): `int h = ((const uint16_t *)w)[i]; ... _mm_cvtsi32_si128(h << 16)`. For h >= 0x8000 (every negative BF16 weight) the shift overflows int, which is UB under C11 6.5.7p4. Reached by finish16 for every row tail (n % 16 != 0). I built with GCC 13.3 in WSL using the CMake HEARTH_ASAN / hxcc --asan POSIX flags (-fsanitize=address,undefined): `tq_asan --no-bench` printed `src/quant_avx2.c:137:53: runtime error: left shift of 32768 by 16 places cannot be represented in type 'int'` (exit 0 because UBSan recovers by default). With `UBSAN_OPTIONS=halt_on_error=1`, test_quant exits 1 (stack: w_one <- finish16 <- mm_float <- mm_bf16_avx2). My own adversarial test hits it too (`left shift of 48915`). Results are still correct with MSVC and GCC today. The engineer's 'no ASan reports' claim rests on MSVC only.
findings.fix_hint: Shift in unsigned: `uint32_t h = ((const uint16_t *)w)[i]; ... _mm_cvtsi32_si128((int)(h << 16))`, or build the vector with _mm_cvtsi32_si128(h) followed by _mm_slli_epi32(.., 16).

findings.title: Cross-ISA bit-identity for Q8/Q4 depends on the caller's MXCSR rounding mode (round-toward-zero breaks it)
findings.evidence: Scalar activation quantization rounds with the magic-number trick q_rint (quant.c:46-49). AVX2 and AVX-512 use _mm256_cvtps_epi32 (quant_avx2.c:100) and _mm512_cvtps_epi32 (quant_avx512.c:99), which follow MXCSR. The two agree under RN, RD and RU. Under RZ, a negative value such as -2.5 becomes -3 in scalar but -2 in SIMD. Scratch test v_t02_adv.c (MSVC /O2, MSVC ASan and GCC -O2 all agree): 'E MXCSR FTZ+DAZ / round-down / round-up: 0 matmul identity failures, 0 act-quant mismatches (40 cases)' but 'E MXCSR round-to-zero: 32 matmul identity failures, 32 act-quant mismatches (40 cases)', e.g. '[round-to-zero] q8 avx2 != scalar: rows 35 cols 192 T 3 (105 values)'. Hearth is a library loaded into a host process (Python/ctypes), so the FP environment belongs to the caller. Under non-default modes the 'authoritative' quantizer output and the 'round-half-to-even' of NUMERICS §2 also change.
findings.fix_hint: Either state the default-FP-environment precondition in NUMERICS and have the public entry points (hearth_matmul/hearth_quantize, later hearth_eval) save MXCSR, force RN, and restore it; or make rounding mode-independent: _mm512_cvt_roundps_epi32(p, _MM_FROUND_TO_NEAREST_INT|_MM_FROUND_NO_EXC), _mm256_round_ps(p, same) before the conversion, and a scalar RNE that does not depend on the mode.

findings.title: hx_act_bytes lacks the 2^40 element cap of hx_row_bytes and returns a wrapped size
findings.evidence: `return (size_t)n * sizeof(float);` has no upper bound. A probe linked against the GCC objects printed: `hx_act_bytes(F32, 2^62+1) = 4`, `hx_act_bytes(F32, 2^62) = 0`, `hx_row_bytes(F32, 2^62+1) = 0`. A caller that sizes an activation buffer with hx_act_bytes(dt, n) and then runs hx_act_prepare or a kernel on n would overflow the heap. It is latent today: the only caller is hearth_matmul, which validates n_cols through hx_row_bytes first, and no other engine module calls it yet (grep).
findings.fix_hint: Apply the same guard as hx_row_bytes: `if (n <= 0 || n > ((int64_t)1 << 40)) return 0;`.

findings.title: Q8 scale saturation deviates from the literal normative NUMERICS §6, and no contract issue was raised for it
findings.evidence: NUMERICS §6: 'Q8: per block d = amax/127 (stored f16), q = nearbyint(x / d_f16) clamped'. For amax > ~8.32e6, f16(amax/127) is inf, so the literal spec gives q = 0 and dequantized NaN. q_scale_f16 (quant.c:68-72), used at quant.c:108, instead stores 0x7bff (65504) and clamps q. My fuzz of 20000 blocks over 2^-45..2^25 against a §6 reference matched exactly only after I added the saturation rule (848 saturated blocks). The behaviour is sensible and documented in a quant.c comment, but the normative doc is silent, and the handover's contract_issues does not propose updating it, although it does for the NaN rule.
findings.fix_hint: Add to contract_issues: NUMERICS §6 'a block scale that overflows f16 is stored as ±65504 (0x7bff/0xfbff); q is then clamped as usual'. The same applies to the Q4 candidate scales.

findings.title: Converter falls back to its own defaults for missing config.json keys, and these differ from the transformers defaults, so a mismatch goes unnoticed
findings.evidence: hearth_meta reads raw config.json with cfg.get(key, default). Its defaults differ from transformers' config classes: n_group 1 vs DeepseekV3Config 8, topk_group 1 vs 4, routed_scaling_factor 1.0 vs 2.5, and rms_norm_eps 1e-6 vs Olmoe/Mixtral 1e-5. rope_params, however, uses the transformers config object, so the defaults are inconsistent within one conversion. Reproduction (scratch o_defaults.py): build the tiny DeepseekV3 test model with HF defaults (n_group=8, topk_group=4, routed_scaling_factor=2.5), save_pretrained, then delete those three keys from config.json. AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained on that directory reports '8 4 2.5'. The converted container has metadata '1 1 1.0'. The Reference vs transformers max abs logit diff is 4.656, against a tolerance of 0.0168. No error or warning is raised. Published DeepSeek-V3/Kimi-K2/Qwen/OLMoE configs include these keys, so no known real checkpoint is affected.
findings.fix_hint: When transformers is available, read the hyper-parameters from _tf_config(cfg), which already exists, instead of from the raw dict. Without transformers, raise ValueError for missing routing keys instead of guessing. Add a test that deletes a defaulted key from config.json and compares against transformers.from_pretrained on the same directory.

findings.title: Reference.eval leaves the KV cache and routing history partly advanced when a later token in the batch is invalid
findings.evidence: eval() runs _forward token by token, and _forward validates each token (vocabulary range and max_seq) only when it reaches it. Scratch j_misc.py on a mixtral make_tiny: ref.eval([1, 2, 999]) raises 'token 999 outside vocabulary of 256'. After that, pos = 2 and routing_history has 2 rows, and a following ref.eval([3]) gives logits different from a fresh evaluation. The caller gets an exception but the state has silently changed.
findings.fix_hint: Validate every token, and pos + len(tokens) <= max_seq, before evaluating any token. Alternatively, snapshot pos and the KV length and roll back on exception.

findings.title: Byte accounting with prefetch on is untested: per-token prefetch, wasted and DRAM bytes can be wrong by orders of magnitude and all 112 tests still pass
findings.evidence: Mutation run (seed 11, core.py lines 144-200,255-395) left M0322 alive: `nv_p = ...sum() / tok` changed to `* tok`. I applied it by hand to a scratch copy and ran the unmodified test file against it: '112 passed in 19.03s'. On that copy, `python -m hearth.sim --model kimi-k2 --tokens 2000 --cache-gb 40 --prefetch 0.8` printed 'NVMe per token 3071655.669 GB (demand 3.682, prefetch 3071651.987 ...)'; SIMULATOR.md §7 has 4.630 GB. Two more hand mutants also gave '112 passed': nvme_prefetch_wasted divided by 7 (core.py:392), and prefetched experts dropped from DRAM bytes (timing.py:251, `dram_b += ... - frac*ph_h*sh`). The cause is in tests/py/test_sim.py:303 (test_prefetch_accounting). It only asserts `b['nvme'] == b['nvme_demand'] + b['nvme_prefetch']`, which is how core.py:391 defines nvme, plus wasted == 0 / > 0. The exact byte test at test_sim.py:255 runs with prefetch off only. SIMULATOR.md §5 (line 507) still says 'The NVMe and DRAM equalities hold' without that restriction. The production code is correct: my scratch check cold_pf.py shows demand + prefetch - wasted == (miss + pfhit) x slab per step, with cold slabs and prefetch together, to a relative error of 4.4e-16.
findings.fix_hint: With prefetch on (and cold_bits), assert exact per-token identities. (a) nvme_demand + nvme_prefetch - nvme_prefetch_wasted == Σ(miss·S + pfhit·S, cold at S_c) / tokens. (b) nvme_prefetch == Σ frac·(issued bytes) / tokens. (c) dram == (loads - vram - skip)·slab + dense backbone. Fix the §5 wording.

findings.title: Golden lock can be re-locked by the change under review; CI passes a gutted golden suite (INV-VERIFY), and the README claim that a change cannot weaken its own check is false
findings.evidence:
In CI, check_golden.py is taken from the PR base (.trusted), but it runs with --root . and so reads tests/golden/MANIFEST.sha256 from the PR head (check_golden.py:173-188 has no base-manifest comparison). Unlike decisions.yml, nothing requires a maintainer label when tests/golden/ or its manifest changes.

Reproduction in a scratch copy (scratchpad/prcopy, containing tests/golden, governance/tools and python/hearth):
1. Replaced test_golden_invariants.py with a stub, 'def test_scheduling_independence(): pass'.
2. Ran `HEARTH_MAINTAINER=1 python governance/tools/check_golden.py --update` (the flag is only an honour system; any agent can set it).
3. Ran the real repo's tool against the copy, as CI does with the base-revision tool:
   - `python -E <repo>/governance/tools/check_golden.py --root .` printed 'golden lock OK: 1 file(s) verified', rc=0.
   - `... --root . --run` printed 'golden suite OK: 1 passed, 0 failed, 0 errors, 0 skipped', rc=0.

So both CI golden steps are green after a contributor deletes every golden test. Separately, pull_request runs use the PR's own ci.yml, so the .trusted mechanism only holds with branch protection plus CODEOWNERS on .github/. The README states that guarantee unconditionally (governance/README.md:102-107: 'a change cannot weaken the check it is judged by'). The engineer's report repeats the claim.
findings.fix_hint: Add a base comparison to check_golden.py, e.g. `--base-manifest <file>` or `--base-rev <rev>`: verify the head's tests/golden files against the BASE manifest, and fail when the manifest or any locked file differs from base unless a maintainer acknowledgement is given. Mirror decisions.yml: a 'golden-reviewed' label workflow, and add tests/golden/MANIFEST.sha256 to the .trusted sparse checkout. State in README/INVARIANTS guidance that the guarantee also needs branch protection and CODEOWNERS on .github/ and tests/golden/. Test it: a temp git repo where HEAD re-locks a modified golden test must fail without the acknowledgement.

findings.title: Decision circuit breaker can be bypassed: duplicate-id shadow files hide retired ADRs, and in-place rewrites of Accepted ADRs are not detected
findings.evidence:
breaker() builds `cur = {a.id: a for ...}`, so the last file with a given id wins.

Probe 1, duplicate ids (scratchpad/adrbase vs adrhead):
- Set all 8 ADRs to '- Status: Deprecated'.
- Added ADR-000N-zz-shadow.md copies with '- Status: Accepted'.
- Ran `python governance/tools/adr.py breaker --root adrhead --base-root adrbase`: 'decision breaker OK: 0 of 8 accepted decisions retired', rc=0.
- Control without the shadow files: 'CIRCUIT BREAKER: 8 of 8 ... (100%)', rc=1.
- Only `adr.py lint` catches the duplicate ids, and CI runs lint from the PR's own (untrusted) governance/tools, not .trusted.

Probe 2, in-place rewrite:
- Changed ADR-0004's title to 'LRU expert eviction by default' and its Decision to 'The default policy is `HEARTH_POLICY_LRU`', keeping it Accepted.
- `adr.py lint` printed 'ADR lint OK'. The breaker printed 'decision breaker OK: 0 of 8 accepted decisions retired', rc=0.
- This contradicts README.md:33 ('Never rewritten in place') and README.md:210 ('Accepted decisions are not edited to mean something else'). Rewriting gets around the 15% churn limit without any review.
findings.fix_hint: In breaker(): count a base-Accepted id as retired unless exactly one current file carries that id and it is Accepted; report duplicate ids as tripping. Trip (or require the decisions-reviewed label) when the Context or Decision of an ADR that was Accepted at base changes in substance. breaker() already computes adrs_changed via _content(). Add tests for both scenarios.

findings.title: ECMA-262 pattern translator is not exact: backreferences to unset groups evaluate differently, and quantified assertions invalid under the 'u' flag are accepted
findings.evidence:
Ran a differential test of ecma_regex() against node v24 `new RegExp(p, 'u')` (scratchpad/ecma_diff.py) on 4,025 random and targeted patterns, each against 10-19 inputs. Results:
- 4 patterns with different match results, all backreferences to a group that did not participate. Example: pattern '^(?:(z)|gen)\1-[0-9]{3,}-[a-z0-9-]+$' with input 'gen-003-governance' gives node 'true', but the translator says no match. Through the CLI, validate_handover --schema backref_schema.json rejects the real T05 manifest under both --engine builtin and jsonschema (rc=1, '0/1 manifest(s) valid').
- 227 patterns that ECMA rejects ('Invalid quantifier' / 'Nothing to repeat') are accepted. Examples: '(?=a)*', '(?<!b)+', '\b{2}', '\B*?'. The CLI accepts a schema with '^(?=gen-)*gen-...' (rc=0), although the docstring promises that syntax ECMA-262 rejects in 'u' mode makes the schema unusable (exit 2).
- 2 patterns crash the translator (OverflowError; see the next finding).

The hand-written ECMA_MATCHES/ECMA_INVALID tests cover neither class.
findings.fix_hint: Reject backreferences (\N and \k<name>) outright, since the handover schema does not need them. The conditional form (?(N)\N) does not fix it either: JS also clears captures on each iteration of a quantified group. In ecma_translate, raise re.error when a quantifier follows a lookaround group, \b, \B, ^ or $. Add these cases to ECMA_INVALID/ECMA_MATCHES, and optionally add a node-based differential test that is skipped when node is absent.

findings.title: Malformed schemas are handled inconsistently: OverflowError traceback with exit 1; with jsonschema installed, per-file failures instead of exit 2; keyword values are not checked
findings.evidence:
Ran scratchpad/schema_probe.py and the CLI against governance/handovers/T05-governance-gen-003.json:
- A pattern with '{3,4294967296}' crashes with an 'OverflowError: the repetition number is too large' traceback, rc=1, under both --engine builtin and auto. Only re.error is caught (lines 358-361 and 679-682), so the exit code says 'invalid manifest' instead of 2.
- '"type": "strin"' gives rc=2 with builtin, but with auto (jsonschema 4.26 installed) gives rc=1 and the per-file error 'validator failed on this file: UnknownType'. The jsonschema path never checks the schema.
- '"required": "generation_id"' (a string) gives rc=1 with builtin, and the error "required property 'g' is missing" printed once per character.
- '"minLength": "5"' raises a TypeError, reported as a per-file failure, rc=1.
The docstring promises exit 2 for an unusable schema.
findings.fix_hint: Catch (re.error, OverflowError, RecursionError) when compiling patterns, both in _check_schema and in main. For the jsonschema engine, call cls.check_schema(schema) in main and map SchemaError to exit 2. In MiniValidator._check_schema, check value types: required must be a list of strings; min*/max* must be non-negative integers or numbers; enum must be a list.

findings.title: friction.py signature normalisation does not mask Windows/MSVC pointer values, so a repeated crash on the primary platform is never detected as thrashing
findings.evidence:
normalize() masks only addresses that start with '0x'. MSVC's printf("%p") prints '00000095F031FCC0', with no prefix (checked by building scratchpad/p.c with hxcc). I recorded 3 attempts with signature 'FAIL test_store.c:211: slot 0x7 ptr

not aligned', where P was 000001F2A3B4C5D6, 00000213B4C5D6E7 and 0000024C1D2E3F40. `friction.py check` printed 'ok (worst open signature: 1/3 failures without a change)', rc=0. The same three attempts with 0x-prefixed pointers were detected ('EPISTEMIC FRICTION ... 3x'). ADR-0007 makes Windows/MSVC the first-class platform.
findings.fix_hint: Also mask long bare hex runs, e.g. re.sub(r'\b[0-9A-Fa-f]{8,16}\b', '<addr>', s) when the run contains a digit, and consider masking temp-dir paths and PIDs. Add a test using an MSVC-style %p signature.

findings.title: A batch of prefetch hints wakes only one reader, so next-layer prefetch runs one read at a time
findings.evidence:
hx_store_prefetch queues all n hints but calls hx_cond_signal(&s->work_cv) once ('if (added) hx_cond_signal'). Only one idle reader wakes. That reader loops through the prefetch queue by itself, and nothing else wakes the other readers: finish() broadcasts work_cv only when starved. The store's own limit pf_inflight_max = n_io-1 is never reached for a batch, and ARCHITECTURE step 3 issues the top-k hints for layer L+1 in one call.

Verifier harness adv_store.c (8 readers, a read hook that sleeps 30 ms and counts concurrent reads, readers idle before the hint):
- 1 prefetch call x 8 ids: max 1 read in flight, all 8 resident after 243 ms.
- 8 prefetch calls x 1 id: max 7 in flight, 62 ms.
- 8 demand misses: max 8 in flight, 31 ms.
This reproduced on MSVC /O2, MSVC ASan and gcc TSan (Linux pthreads, 242 ms).

On the real NVMe (adv_bench.c: 990 PRO, direct I/O, cold, top-8 batches, readers 4/8/16, GB/s):
- 2.39 MiB slabs: one call 4.78/4.34/4.82; one id per call 5.81/6.57/6.13; demands 6.47/6.28/6.49.
- 22.3 MiB slabs: one call 5.58/5.70/5.55; one id per call 6.95/6.41/6.15; demands 7.04/6.45/6.09.
The machine was shared, so these numbers are noisy.

The suite cannot see this. pf_queue_limit hints one id per call (each call signals). A mutant replacing the signal with hx_cond_broadcast survives: test_store --quick seed 3 gives 45132 checks, 0 failed. With that change, the probe shows 7 reads in flight and 62 ms.
findings.fix_hint: Wake one reader per queued hint: call hx_cond_signal once per added key, or hx_cond_broadcast when added > 1. Alternatively, in next_job, after taking a prefetch job, signal work_cv if pfq_len > 0 and pf_inflight < pf_inflight_max. Add a test that issues one hx_store_prefetch call with K ids to K idle readers (read hook counting concurrency) and asserts min(K, n_io-1) reads in flight.

findings.title: Overcommit test precondition is flaky under CPU oversubscription
findings.evidence:
The settle loop at lines 719-725 counts a resident-prefix length of 0 as 'settled'. If the readers are not scheduled within about 20 polls x 2 ms, head stays 0 and CHECK(head > 0 && head < n) fails, although the store is fine. It failed only under CPU oversubscription.

With 32 busy loops ('python burn.py', one per logical CPU) plus 6 parallel 'test_store.exe --quick --seed N':
- seeds 61-66: 2 of 6 failed;
- seeds 81-86: 3 of 6 failed.
Every failure was 'test_store.c:726: overcommit: 0 of 80 served before starving'.

findings.title: A stale miss_pending flag from an abandoned demand under-counts later misses and hits
findings.evidence:
miss_pending[key] is cleared only by take() or a failed demand read. If a demanded slab is never collected (its hold expires at the tick and it is later evicted), the flag stays set across tokens. A later genuine cold read of that expert is then not counted as a miss (request_demand line 399), and its use is not counted as a hit (take line 379). The stale flag also makes mark_fresh treat an unrelated later completion of that key as news.

Verifier harness adv_store.c:
- An expert demanded and abandoned, then evicted by LRU churn, then acquired again: 'reads 1 misses 0 hits 0 stall_ns 24100'.
- An abandoned demand followed 2 ticks later by 2 resident acquisitions (after reset_stats): 'hits 1 misses 0'.
The statistics hits/(hits+misses) are what the policy comparison and the simulator calibration use.
findings.fix_hint: In assign(), when evicting a READY slot, clear miss_pending[old key] and unfresh it. Alternatively, clear miss_pending for uncollected demands at hx_store_tick. Add a stats test for this abandoned-demand sequence.

findings.title: Passing sec to check_regions is a C11 constraint violation (pointer to array with added const)
findings.evidence: `uint64_t sec[4][2]` is passed to the parameter `const uint64_t sec[4][2]` (type `const uint64_t (*)[2]`). Before C2x this implicit conversion is not allowed. gcc 13.3 with -std=c11 -Wall -Wextra -pedantic reports: 'src/modelfile.c:718:32: warning: invalid use of pointers to arrays with different qualifiers in ISO C before C2X [-Wpedantic]'. The file is clean at -Wall -Wextra and MSVC /W3, so INV-SAFE is met; this is a portability and conformance nit only.
findings.fix_hint: Declare the local as `const uint64_t sec[4][2] = {...}` at line 716.

engineer_open_issues: Awaiting a maintainer decision: hx_store_acquire returns NULL for an unreadable expert (until the next tick), against the header. T07/T08 must treat NULL as an I/O error.

findings.title: Some malformed request bodies crash the handler thread with no HTTP response (deep JSON nesting, integer literals over 4300 digits)
findings.evidence: Handler._body catches only (UnicodeDecodeError, json.JSONDecodeError). Command: PYTHONPATH=python python scratchpad/v3/http_edge.py, which sends raw requests to make_server(FakeEngine). Results: body b'['*200000 gave status line b'' (connection dropped) and stderr showed 'RecursionError: maximum recursion depth exceeded while decoding a JSON array'. A body with "max_tokens": 9...9 (5000 digits) also gave b'' with 'ValueError: Exceeds the limit (4300 digits) for integer string conversion'. Both print a full traceback through socketserver.handle_error. The gate and KV bookkeeping were unaffected (assert_synced passed afterwards, busy=False).
findings.fix_hint: In _body, catch (ValueError, RecursionError) around json.loads (JSONDecodeError is a ValueError subclass) and raise HTTPError(400, 'invalid JSON body').

findings.title: Anthropic /v1/messages: a system text block whose 'text' is not a string raises TypeError, and the client gets no response
findings.evidence: Request: POST /v1/messages {"system":[{"type":"text","text":5}],"messages":[{"role":"user","content":"a"}],"max_tokens":2}. The connection closed with an empty reply, and stderr showed 'TypeError: sequence item 0: expected str instance, int found' from "".join(b.get('text','') ...). Related looseness: system blocks that are not dicts or not of type text are silently ignored ([1,2] gives 200). A non-string message role ("role": 5 on /v1/chat/completions) is accepted with 200 and rendered as role '5'.
findings.fix_hint: Validate each system block: it must be a dict with type 'text' and a str 'text', else HTTPError(400). In normalize_messages or _chat, require role to be a str from the allowed set.

findings.title: A queued request whose client has disconnected still runs its full generation (confirmed; the engineer disclosed it)
findings.evidence: scratchpad/v3/queued_dead.py: request A holds the engine. Request B (non-stream, max_tokens=2000) waits in the queue, and B's client closes its socket before A finishes. After A was released, the counters read completion_tokens=2003 (3 for A + 2000 for B), so the engine generated every token for a client that was gone. On a 1T model at 1-5 tok/s that is many minutes of engine time. The OpenAI SDK retries automatically on timeout, so each abandoned retry queues another full generation.
findings.fix_hint: Before generating (after gate.acquire) and between tokens for non-stream requests, poll the socket (select plus MSG_PEEK, where recv returning b'' means the peer closed) and abort. Optionally add EngineGate.acquire(timeout) as well.

findings.title: Engine accepts bytes paths in its type check but crashes with AttributeError
findings.evidence: _encode_path does os.fspath(p).encode('utf-8'). For bytes input os.fspath returns bytes, which has no .encode. Engine.__init__ explicitly treats bytes as a path (isinstance(mirrors, (str, bytes, os.PathLike))). scratchpad/v3/edge.py on the real DLL: Engine(os.fsencode(model)) gave AttributeError: 'bytes' object has no attribute 'encode', and so did mirrors=[b'...'] and mirrors=b'...'. PYTHON_API only requires str/Path, so this is a robustness and consistency issue.
findings.fix_hint: p = os.fspath(p); return p if isinstance(p, bytes) else p.encode('utf-8'). Alternatively, raise TypeError for bytes, consistently, including in the mirrors check.

findings.title: At an independent mutation seed, scores fall below the reported ones; the surviving mutants include real test gaps
findings.evidence: Command: mutate.py --max-mutants 24 --jobs 4 --seed 29 --timeout 240 --test "{python} -m pytest -q -x -p no:cacheprovider tests/py/test_runtime.py", with HEARTH_LIB set. All three files scored 91.7%. generate.py had 2 survivors: M0148 is equivalent (range(0,...)), but M0263 changes 'len(prompt) > cap' to '>=' at generate.py:313, so a prompt that exactly fills the KV cache would be rejected and no test notices. server.py had 2 survivors: M0443 changes the /v1/completions default max_tokens 16 to 17 (server.py:659, untested), and M0266 changes '<=' to '<' in _drain's limit at server.py:444 (boundary). chat.py had 2 survivors: M0297 and M0298 in Conversation.say, where 'reply.append(d)' after ts.finish() is deleted. With that mutant the flushed tail of a reply is streamed to the user but dropped from conversation history, for example text held back as a possible '<|im_end|>' prefix or an incomplete UTF-8 character. The engineer reports 100% for chat.py and server.py at seeds 3/11 and says every survivor is equivalent; that holds only for those samples. My generate.py run also hit the M0370 timeout, which the engineer documents as a real infinite loop.
findings.fix_hint: Add tests for: generate() with len(prompt) == kv_capacity, which yields one token and then finishes with 'length'; /v1/completions without max_tokens returning exactly 16 tokens; and Conversation.say recording a reply whose tail is only released by ts.finish(), e.g. a reply ending in '<' under the ChatML fallback, by asserting messages[-1]['content'] equals the concatenated stream.

findings.title: CLI argument edge cases escape main()'s error mapping or are not validated
findings.evidence: 'python -m hearth serve tiny.hearth --port 99999' opens the engine and then dies with a full traceback ending 'OverflowError: bind(): port must be 0-65535.' (OverflowError is not mapped, and the port is not range-checked before the possibly slow model open). 'hearth bench --prompt-tokens -5' prints 'hearth bench: ValueError: negative dimensions are not allowed' (a numpy message), with no validation of negative counts. 'serve --max-queue -1' is silently treated as 0.

findings.title: POSIX (macOS) portability, by inspection: test_cli_doctor_text_report assumes 'available' RAM, which _ram() cannot provide on macOS
findings.evidence: CONTRIBUTING.md lists Linux/macOS as build platforms. On macOS _ram() falls back to sysconf and returns {'total': ...} only (cli.py:552-554), so doctor prints 'X total' without 'available'. The test asserts the regex '... total, [\d.]+ \w+ available$' (line 2932) and rep['ram']['total'] >= rep['ram'].get('available', 0) > 0 (line 2950); both fail when 'available' is absent. findings.fix_hint: Make the assertions conditional on 'available' being present. Optionally read available memory on macOS via sysctl/vm_stat, or report total only.

findings.title: prefetch_extra near INT_MAX is accepted, then overflows a signed int (undefined behaviour) and silently turns prefetch off
findings.evidence: api.c:99 only rejects prefetch_extra < 0, and model.c:1550 stores the value unclamped. prefetch_next computes `imin(m->K + m->prefetch_extra, m->E)`. My probe.c, built with gcc 13 and -fsanitize=address,undefined in WSL and run on a tiny deepseek_v3 Q4 container with prefetch_extra = INT_MAX, prints: `engine/src/model.c:903:20: runtime error: signed integer overflow: 4 + 2147483647 cannot be represented in type 'int'` (stack: prefetch_next <- moe_layer <- forward <- hx_model_eval <- hearth_eval). Effect: kk becomes negative, so the gate test `pf_prec >= 0.5*K/kk` always passes but zero experts are predicted. 'prefetch issued' is 0 for INT_MAX and INT_MAX-3, but 180 for 2^30. A user asking for 'prefetch everything' gets no prefetch. Logits stayed correct and nothing crashed. This violates INV-SAFE's 'runs clean under sanitizers' for an input the API accepts.
findings.fix_hint: After setup_dims in hx_model_open, clamp: m->prefetch_extra = imin(o->prefetch_extra, m->E). Alternatively compute kk as (extra >= E - K ? E : K + extra).

findings.title: Required non-output behaviours are untested: 5 targeted mutants of model.c survive the full test_model run
findings.evidence:
I applied each mutant to a scratch copy of model.c, built it with hxcc together with the unchanged test_model.c, and ran it with seed 1. Every one reports 'test_model: 1098 checks, 0 failed':
- M1: model.c:1163 calls hx_store_tick once per forward call instead of once per token. The spec says 'hx_store_tick once per evaluated token'.
- M2: model.c:983 adds T*K to expert_loads_unique instead of nu. The check at test_model.c:750 (`>= 4 && <= expert_uses`) still passes when unique == uses.
- M3: model.c:1054 stops accumulating stall_ns. The check at test_model.c:756 (`stall <= moe`) is satisfied by 0.
- M4: model.c:944 makes PREFETCH_NEXT predict with the current layer's router (w->router) instead of layer L+1's.
- M7: model.c:998 makes PREFETCH_SHARED predict from h without adding the shared-expert output.
The stats and prefetch-prediction rules from the spec are therefore not pinned by any test. The code as written is correct by inspection: on the synthetic q30 container with a 4 GiB cache, prefetch was 23113 used of 24786 issued.
findings.fix_hint: Assert expert_loads_unique exactly. For one decode token it equals n_moe*top_k; for a batch, count distinct ids per MoE layer from the trace. Assert stall_s > 0 when cache_gb = 0 with a slowed read hook. Check that ticks advance per token, e.g. LFU heat decays by decay^T after T tokens through a store seam. For prefetch, use a container whose layer L+1 router depends only on the residual, and assert prefetch_used/prefetch_issued above a threshold for NEXT and SHARED. Also assert the predicted set equals the naive reference's top-k for layer L+1's router on rmsnorm(h [+ rs*shared], ffn_norm[L+1]).

findings.title: hearth_trace_start on the open model's own path truncates the model file
findings.evidence: Python Engine (HEARTH_LIB = my scratch DLL), on a copy of a tiny Q4 container with cache_gb=0: trace_start(<model path>) is accepted. The next eval fails with 'hearth_eval failed (code -4)', and the file on disk is now 24 bytes (SHA-1 changed). hx_file_open(WRITE|CREATE) truncates and Windows sharing allows it while the engine holds the file open. There is no crash, but a caller's slip destroys a model file that can be hundreds of GB. A mirror path would be truncated the same way.
findings.fix_hint: In hx_model_trace_start, refuse a path equal to the model path or any mirror path. Better, compare file identity through a platform helper. Or open without truncation and refuse an existing non-empty file that does not start with the HRTR magic.

findings.title: verbose is process-wide and sticky: a later engine opened with verbose=0 keeps logging INFO/DEBUG
findings.evidence: Python, three engines in sequence on the same container. Engine A (verbose=0) prints nothing. Engine B (verbose=2) prints '[hearth] expert store: ...' and other lines. Engine C (verbose=0, opened after B is closed) still prints the same INFO/DEBUG lines. hearth.h documents verbose per engine as '0 quiet, 1 info, 2 debug'. api.c only ever raises the global level, so nothing short of setting HEARTH_LOG makes an engine quiet again. This affects multi-engine hosts such as server.py and the tests.
findings.fix_hint: Either restore the previous level in hearth_close, or treat verbose as a per-engine override. The latter needs a per-engine log gate, which would be a contract change in hx_platform.h. At minimum, document in hearth.h that verbose sets the process log level and never lowers it.

findings.title: Attention value passes (MLA and GQA) are slow at long context, and MLA attention cost becomes comparable to NVMe time on the target DeepSeek/Kimi shapes
findings.evidence:
hearth-bench, 16 threads, fully cached, shared machine (load 44-94%).
- Synthetic Qwen3-30B-A3B container: decode attention phase is 20.3 ms/token at a 64-token context and 41 ms/token at 3000. Prefill of 3000 tokens runs at 165 tok/s, with attention 12.3 s of 18.1 s, against 370-404 tok/s for a 512-token prefill.
- 6-layer DeepSeek-V3-shaped MLA container (make_shaped dict preset, D 7168, H 128, C 512, physical_experts 16): decode attention goes from 23.6 ms/token at context 64 to 42.9 ms/token at 1550, i.e. +3.2 ms per MLA layer per token, or about +195 ms/token extrapolated to 61 layers. Prefill of 1500 tokens runs at 55 tok/s, with attention 16.3 s of 27.3 s.
- Rough estimate: about 215 M multiply-adds per layer in 3.2 ms is about 4 GMAC/s per thread. mla_values (model.c:653-671) and gqa_values (model.c:515) are plain C loops in a TU built without /arch, and mla_softmax uses scalar hx_dot16.
The brief sets no MLA speed target, and the engineer listed the GQA value pass and the missing MLA benchmarks as open issues.
findings.fix_hint: Add an ISA-dispatched canonical axpy kernel (y_i = y_i + a*x_i, mul then add, no FMA) to hx_kernels in quant.c and use it in gqa_values and mla_values. Vectorising across d/c keeps each element's sequential-in-t order, so results stay bit-identical. Use the F32 matmul kernel or a dispatched dot16 for the q_pe·kpe term. For prefill, reuse each cache row across the tokens of a sub-batch in the value pass.

findings.title: Per-activation hit counting makes batched (prefill) hit rates misleading as a cache metric
findings.evidence: The extra try_acquire/release loop at model.c:1019 counts n-1 hits for every expert shared by n tokens in a batch. On a cold cache with a 20 GiB budget, hearth-bench --prompt 512 reports 'prefill 512 tok ... hit 97.3% | read 15.399 GB', even though every needed slab was read from NVMe. With a 26-slot minimum cache, a 64-token prefill reports 'hit 79.2%' while reading all 5271 unique loads (13.2 GB). This is the documented choice (heat and usage_out now independent of batching, matching hearth.sim's per-load definition), but the bench's 'hit' column no longer says anything about the cache for prefill.
findings.fix_hint: In hearth-bench, also print a per-unique-load hit rate, e.g. 1 - reads/expert_loads_unique, or bytes_read/(expert_loads_unique*slab). Document both definitions in hearth.h as the engineer's contract_issue proposes.
